title: Java HashMap
learningObjectives: Create a HashMap with key and value types.
Insert and retrieve mappings with put and get.
Check keys and provide default values safely.
Understand unique keys and unspecified iteration order.

understand.concept: HashMap stores key-value mappings and implements Map. Keys are unique; putting a value for an existing key replaces its previous value. HashMap permits one null key and null values, and it does not guarantee iteration order. Use get to retrieve a value, containsKey to distinguish a missing key from a key mapped to null, and getOrDefault for a fallback. Keys should have stable equals and hashCode behaviour while stored.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic helps Java developers select and use the right standard-library tools for java hashmap in maintainable applications.
understand.analogy: Think of the collection or date API as a purpose-built tool: its operations communicate the guarantees your program can rely on.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a guide; Java API contracts, equality rules and exception behaviour determine the actual result.

explain.narrative: Declare both generic types, for example HashMap<String, Integer>. put adds or replaces a mapping; get retrieves by key; remove deletes a mapping. keySet, values and entrySet expose views for iteration. Do not rely on display order. For custom key classes, implement equals and hashCode consistently and avoid mutating fields that participate in hashing while the key is in the map.

examples.title: Create mappings
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(); stock.put("Pen", 12); stock.put("Book", 5); System.out.println(stock.get("Pen")); } }
examples.explanation: put stores a value under a key and get retrieves it.

examples.title: Replace an existing key
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>(); scores.put("Asha", 70); scores.put("Asha", 85); System.out.println(scores.get("Asha")); System.out.println(scores.size()); } }
examples.explanation: A map can contain only one mapping for a given key.

examples.title: Use a default value
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<String, String> codes = new HashMap<>(); codes.put("IN", "India"); System.out.println(codes.getOrDefault("US", "Unknown")); } }
examples.explanation: getOrDefault returns a fallback when a key has no mapping.

examples.title: Check before retrieving
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<Integer, String> users = new HashMap<>(); users.put(7, "Mina"); System.out.println(users.containsKey(7)); System.out.println(users.containsKey(9)); } }
examples.explanation: containsKey checks whether a mapping exists.

examples.title: Iterate over entries
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<String, Integer> points = new HashMap<>(); points.put("A", 2); points.put("B", 3); int sum = 0; for (var entry : points.entrySet()) sum += entry.getValue(); System.out.println(sum); } }
examples.explanation: entrySet exposes key-value entries; this example does not assume an order.

questions.explanation: Map associates each key with a value.

questions.prompt: Can a HashMap contain duplicate keys?
questions.answer: No; a new value replaces the old mapping
options: No; a new value replaces the old mapping
questions.explanation: Each key identifies at most one mapping.

questions.prompt: Which method checks whether a key exists?
questions.explanation: containsKey checks for a mapping with the given key.

questions.prompt: Why should equals and hashCode agree for custom keys?
questions.answer: Equal keys must be placed and found consistently
options: Equal keys must be placed and found consistently
questions.explanation: The hash-based lookup relies on compatible equals and hashCode implementations.
